planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees, in a site separate from the typical blue form so the white drift reads cleanly.

directions: Alba is a long-known white-flowered color break of the English bluebell, occurring occasionally in wild woodland populations and maintained in cultivation as a named selection rather than a modern hybrid introduction. It carries the same one-sided, nodding raceme and sweet fragrance as the typical violet-blue form, but with pure white, waxy bells and pale cream anthers that glow in deep woodland shade. Grow it exactly as the species, in humus-rich soil under a deciduous canopy, and let it self-seed into slowly expanding drifts; keep it apart from blue-flowered stands at first if a solid white patch is the goal, since it will cross back toward blue over generations. Foliage dies back fully by midsummer and the site should not be disturbed afterward.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; rarer in the trade than the white form, so source from a reputable specialist bulb supplier.

directions: Rosea is the soft pink color form of the English bluebell, a naturally occurring variant found scattered among wild blue populations and propagated as a distinct named strain for gardeners wanting to echo an old-woodland palette beyond the familiar violet-blue. Growth habit, one-sided drooping racemes, and sweet scent match the species exactly, with only the pale dusty-pink petal color setting it apart. It is slower to bulk up in commerce than the white form and is best treated as a specialty planting mixed sparingly among the typical blue drifts rather than as a solid mass. Give it the same humus-rich, undisturbed woodland bed and allow foliage to die back naturally through early summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in well-drained, humus-enriched soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Alba is the standard white-flowered selection of the vigorous Spanish bluebell, carrying the same upright, many-flowered stems as the typical blue-violet species but in clean white, and is one of the most widely offered named color forms sold by mainstream fall bulb catalogs. It naturalizes with the same ease as the species, spreading by offsets and self-seeding into broad colonies under deciduous canopy, and mixes well with blue or pink Spanish bluebells for a layered mid-spring display. Because it hybridizes freely with the true native English bluebell (H. non-scripta), avoid planting it near naturalized wild bluebell populations. Allow the strap-like foliage to yellow and die back fully before tidying the bed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in well-drained, humus-enriched soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Rosea is the pink-flowered selection of Spanish bluebell, bearing the same upright, loosely one-sided racemes of bell-shaped flowers as the species but in a soft dusty pink that reads warmer than the typical blue-violet form. It is commonly sold alongside the blue and white forms by fall bulb merchants as part of a mixed Spanish bluebell planting and shares the same vigorous, easy-naturalizing habit under deciduous trees. It spreads readily by offset bulbs and self-sown seedlings, so give it room among other shade bulbs rather than a tightly bordered bed. As with other Spanish bluebell forms, keep it away from wild stands of native English bluebell to prevent hybridization.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; this is the common garden bluebell found in most urban and suburban UK and Pacific Northwest plantings, intermediate between its two parent species.

directions: Hyacinthoides x massartiana is the fertile hybrid between the native English bluebell and the introduced Spanish bluebell, and it is in fact the bluebell most often sold and grown in gardens, since it arises wherever the two parents grow near each other and the resulting offspring are vigorous and highly fertile. Its flower stems are more upright than the drooping, strictly one-sided English bluebell but less rigidly erect than the Spanish bluebell, with blooms carried part-way around the stem and a fragrance that is fainter than the true native species. It naturalizes aggressively by both offsets and seed, which is precisely the concern conservationists raise: where it spreads into woodlands holding genuinely wild H. non-scripta, it can swamp the native gene pool over time through continued backcrossing. It is an easy, reliable shade bulb for an ordinary garden setting, but gardeners near protected native bluebell woods should avoid introducing it nearby.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink Star bears soft, clear pink star-shaped flowers, lighter than the deep rose of 'Charmer' and the magenta of 'Radar'.

directions: Soak the knobby tubers briefly before planting 2 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Pink Star produces a gentler, clearer pink star-shaped bloom than the deeper rose-pink of 'Charmer' or the bold magenta-and-white 'Radar', giving it a softer presence when massed with white or pale blue anemone blanda forms. It flowers in early to mid spring, closing its daisy-like petals at night and in overcast conditions, then spreads gradually by tuberous rhizomes into a slowly thickening carpet before going summer-dormant. Once established beneath a deciduous canopy it needs no routine care and resents being disturbed or divided unnecessarily.
